name: Autumn crocus
notes: Not a true crocus. Spring garden crocus (Crocus species) is far less toxic. Chickens usually avoid bitter plants when they have plenty of other forage. Risk rises in bare runs, when prunings are thrown in, or when plants are dried into hay or bedding.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Avocado tree
notes: Birds are among the most sensitive animals to persin. Guatemalan types such as Hass are reported as most toxic. Keep fallen leaves and fruit away from the flock.

name: Bittersweet nightshade
notes: A climbing weed of hedges and fences with purple flowers and red berries. Common in both the US and UK.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Black locust
notes: Poisoning of poultry that ate the seeds or bark has been reported. The flowers are less toxic.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Black nightshade
notes: Common garden weed with white flowers and black berries. Toxin levels vary a lot between plants and with ripeness.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Boxwood
notes: Bitter, so rarely eaten. Do not throw hedge trimmings into the run.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Bracken fern
notes: Harm comes from eating it over time. Most reports are in cattle and horses. Do not use dried bracken as bedding where birds will eat it.

name: Buttercups
notes: Very bitter and blistering, so animals rarely eat much. Drying into hay makes it harmless.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Castor bean
toxic_parts: whole plant to a lesser degree
notes: Grown as an ornamental. The seeds are among the most toxic plant materials known. Remove from any area birds can reach.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Cherry laurel
notes: Common hedge in the UK and US. Wilted leaves after trimming are the most dangerous. Never throw laurel clippings into a run.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Wild black cherry and chokecherry
notes: A classic livestock poison after storms break branches. The ripe fruit flesh is not the danger; the pit, leaves and bark are.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Clematis
notes: Bitter and irritating, so animals rarely eat much.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Cocklebur
notes: Seedlings and burs are the risk. Poisoning is best documented in pigs and cattle, with poultry reports as well.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Coffee senna
compound: anthraquinone derivatives (dianthrones), mostly in the seeds
notes: A weed of the southern US and tropics. Poultry have been poisoned by feed contaminated with its seeds.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Corn cockle
notes: Historically poisoned poultry through contaminated grain. Now rare in farm crops but sold in wildflower mixes.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Rattlebox (crotalaria)
signs: death after weeks or months of exposure
notes: A weed of the southern US. Seed contaminating grain has caused serious poultry losses.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Daffodil
notes: The bulbs hold the most toxin. Chickens scratching up stored or planted bulbs is the usual risk.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Daphne
scientific_name: Daphne mezereum and other Daphne spp.
notes: Garden shrub with scented flowers and red berries.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
IVIS, Guide to Poisonous House and Garden Plants

name: Deadly nightshade
notes: Mostly a UK and European plant. Remove it from any area birds can reach.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Delphinium and larkspur
notes: Garden and wild species. Young plants are the most toxic.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: English ivy
notes: Bitter. Large amounts are needed to cause harm.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Foxglove
notes: Very common in UK gardens and hedgerows. Stays toxic when dried.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Hellebore (Christmas rose)
notes: Winter-flowering garden plant. Sources differ on how dangerous it is: NC State rates the poison severity high, while ASPCA lists mainly gut signs. Treat it as a plant to keep out of reach.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Horse chestnut and buckeye
notes: Do not confuse with edible sweet chestnut (Castanea).

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Hound's tongue
signs: death after weeks or months of exposure
notes: Liver damage builds up over time. Dangerous in hay.

name: Hyacinth
notes: Mostly a risk when bulbs are dug up.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Jimsonweed
notes: Spiny seed pods. Seeds contaminating grain have poisoned poultry and livestock.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Laburnum
notes: Common UK garden tree with yellow hanging flowers. Pods fall into runs in late summer.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
IVIS, Guide to Poisonous House and Garden Plants

name: Lantana
notes: Invasive in warm US states. Most poisoning reports are in cattle.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Lily of the valley
notes: Shade garden plant that spreads by roots.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Lupins
notes: Garden and wild lupins. Sweet lupin varieties bred for feed are low in alkaloids.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Milkweed
compound: cardiac glycosides (cardenolides); some narrow-leaved species carry neurotoxins instead
notes: Planted for monarch butterflies in the US. Narrow-leaved species are the most toxic.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Monkshood
scientific_name: Aconitum napellus and other Aconitum spp.
notes: One of the most toxic garden plants in the UK and US.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Morning glory
compound: indole (ergoline) alkaloids such as lysergic acid amide
notes: Seeds are the main concern. Chicken-specific evidence is limited.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
IVIS, Guide to Poisonous House and Garden Plants

name: Mountain laurel
notes: Evergreen shrub of the eastern US. Stays green in winter when other forage is scarce.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Oak
notes: Serious poisoning is mostly seen in cattle and horses eating large amounts. Chickens nibbling a few acorns is common, but heavy eating is best prevented.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Oleander
notes: Common in warm US states. Small amounts can be fatal. Keep prunings well away from the flock.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Pieris (Japanese andromeda)
notes: Popular evergreen garden shrub in the UK and US.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Poison hemlock
notes: Tall weed with purple-spotted stems and a mousy smell. Poultry poisoning has been reported.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Pokeweed
notes: Wild birds eat the berries, but poisoning of turkeys and other poultry has been reported. Roots are most toxic.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Potato plant
notes: Keep birds out of potato beds and away from sprouting or green potatoes.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Privet
compound: glycosides (terpenoid glycosides and syringin, also called ligustrin)
notes: Common hedge. Serious poisoning in animals is uncommon.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Common ragwort
signs: death after weeks or months of exposure
notes: Listed as an injurious weed in the UK. Damage builds up over time and is not reversible.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Rhododendron and azalea
notes: Very common garden shrubs. Fallen leaves and trimmings are the usual risk.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Rhubarb plant
notes: Leaves are the main danger. Oxalates also bind the calcium hens need for shells.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Rosary pea
notes: Tropical vine, invasive in Florida. Red and black seeds.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Sweet pea
signs: skeletal and blood vessel problems with long exposure
notes: Garden flower. Harm comes from repeated eating of the seeds. The edible garden pea (Pisum) is safe.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Tobacco
notes: Includes ornamental flowering tobacco. Also keep cigarette ends out of runs.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Tomato plant
notes: Ripe red fruit is safe. Birds usually avoid the strong-smelling leaves, but fence them out of tomato beds.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Tulip
toxic_parts: to a lesser degree leaves and flowers
notes: The bulbs are the main risk.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Water hemlock
notes: Grows in wet ground and ditches. Considered the most toxic plant in North America. UK relative hemlock water dropwort (Oenanthe crocata) is similar.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Wisteria
notes: Pods drop in fall and can fall into runs.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

name: Yew
notes: Common in UK churchyards and US landscaping. Often causes sudden death with few signs. The red flesh of the berry is less toxic but the seed inside is deadly. Never throw clippings into a run.

sources.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
